newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain, France await world backing for Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: Spain, France await world backing for Zaire force.

text.p: Spain and France want to send a multinational force of at least 5,000 troops as part of their plan to open humanitarian corridors for a million starving refugees in Zaire, the Spanish Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
French and Spanish leaders discussed the plan at a summit on Monday and Tuesday in Marseille.
"It is a concrete proposal by France and Spain. In the first phase, the troops will secure humanitarian corridors for food and medicine," said a ministry spokesman who asked not to be named.
A minimum of 5,000 soldiers would be needed for the operation to save refugees deprived of food by fighting between Zairean troops and Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels, he added.

France would send about 1,000 troops, Spain would send fewer than 1,000 and the two countries hoped the United States and other nations would contribute thousands more. But no other nations had committed themselves yet to sending troops, the spokesman said.
Britain has said it was too early to know if it would join the force but it would discuss the proposal at a summit with France on Friday.

Belgium said it would not send troops. "Belgium is prepared to lend financial and logistical support to a humanitarian operation...but given our historical ties with the region and recent experience in Rwanda in 1994 it will not be possible to put troops on the ground," said a Belgian Foreign Ministry spokesman.
The Franco-Spanish initiative envisages three phases.
"The idea is little by little, the troops will be replaced by Africans," the spokesman said. "In the second phase, it will be international troops with Africans, in the third phase only Africans."
France and Spain are awaiting international backing for sending troops, particularly from the United States but also from the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.
The United States has not been devoting much attention to the crisis in central Africa because of its presidential election this week.
International aid workers have pleaded for urgent world action to avert a humanitarian disaster, but any relief plan faces enormous obstacles.
Aid workers in the area say they have lost track of the fleeing refugees' precise whereabouts in eastern Zaire.
Urgently requested satellite photographs to assess the situation have failed to materialise.
Meanwhile, time is running out for young, old, weak and ill refugees threatened by hunger, thirst, disease and exposure. Their food supplies are dwindling.
A further complication arose on Wednesday when Zaire said it did not want food distributed to the refugees from its soil.
African diplomats are due to meet in Ethiopia next Monday to discuss a plan for a protection force.
